newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire signs big copper deal despite war. [CORRECTED 13:00 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Zaire signs big copper deal despite war. [CORRECTED 13:00 GMT]

text.p: Zaire's state-owned copper giant Gecamines on Sunday signed its first major joint venture with a foreign company, the Swiss-based Groupe Lundin, despite a spreading civil war in the east of the country.
"This is the rebirth of Zaire's mining industry," Groupe Lundin chairman Adolf Lundin (corrects spelling of Lundin's first name) told Reuters.
"Everything was finally signed and sealed between three and four this morning," said Lundin official Charlie Pettifer.

Groupe Lundin, representing the Canadian company Eurocan Consolidated Ventures, won agreement on Friday from the Zaire government to mine vast resources of copper and cobalt at Tenke Fungurume in the southern Shaba province.

Pettifer told Reuters the final accord with Gecamines was delayed until the early hours of Sunday as four government ministers had to initial about 2,000 pages of contract documents in French and English.
In an interview with Reuters before the ceremony in Kinshasa, Lundin brushed aside the risk of investing in Zaire.
"If you are in resource business, you have to work in the countries that give results. Taking risks too much into account is like competing in a marathon with a broken leg," he said.
Shaba borders the province of South Kivu, large parts of which have been captured in the past two months by Rwanda-backed rebels led by Laurent Kabila, himself a native of Shaba.
The mineral-rich province has tried several times to seceede in Zaire's turbulent post-independence history.
President Mobutu Sese Seko has often claimed to be the one man holding together the vast Central African country of over 300 ethnic groups and about the size of Western Europe.
For more than three months Mobutu has been absent from Zaire, receiving treatment for cancer in Europe.
Regional analysts fear that if he were to die, Zaire's future as a state would be threatened in the bitter succession struggle that could ensue.
But Lundin remains unperturbed.
"We have an international agreement that would prevail," he said.
His group says it will organise security for the mines in coordination with their state partner, Gecamines.
Gecamines already employs South African security guards to prevent theft and smuggling from existing copper and cobalt mines in the Kolwezi and Likazi areas of Shaba.
Under the terms of Sunday's accord Consolidated Eurocan Ventures, in which Lundin is a major shareholder, will own 55 per cent of Tenke Fungurume project, and Gecamine 45 percent.
The deal could lead to further foreign investments in the huge, scarcely tapped mineral potential of Zaire.
"We know already that there were 10 other companies queueing up behind us in this venture," says Lundin.
According to studies already undertaken on site, Tenke Fungurume could become one of the world's largest open-cast copper mines.
"We expect the first phase of production to start by the year 2000. In that phase we hope to produce 100,000 tonnes of copper and 8,000 tonnes of cobalt annually," Lundin told Reuters.
By 2010 the mine could produce as much as 400,000 tonnes of copper a year with resources lasting for up to 100 years, Lundin says.
Feasibility studies for the project will begin in the first quarter of 1997.
